proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: First justify neat cut geometry without assuming transversality of the given proper disks. A smooth handlebody means a manifold diffeomorphic to the standard ball with finitely many smooth one-handles. This model embeds in $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$: take a round ball with finitely many disjoint pairs of small boundary windows and join each pair by a disjoint thin tube outside the ball, choosing the core arcs successively in separate heights and shrinking the tubes. Product window coordinates and corner rounding give the standard smooth one-handle attachments. Transport the actual handlebody and the given disks by one such parametrization and embedding. Apply [F4] to these embedded disk witnesses; their supplied ball cuts are in particular topological balls. Pull the new neat witnesses and the resulting cut-ball parametrizations and product collars back to the actual handlebody. Their boundary circles are EXACTLY the original ones, so the surface, the transverse curve system, and every desired complex-model conclusion are unchanged. This changes only auxiliary compression witnesses; it does not claim an ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism converting the original tangency to a transverse intersection. Cutting along these neat replacement disks presents $\Sigma$ as the surface $P$ obtained from the boundary sphere of the cut ball by removing the interiors of its $2h$ disk faces, with paired boundary identifications $g_i:\partial E_i^+\to\partial E_i^-$. Choose one smooth parametrization of that ball by the standard ball; this is one finite choice permitted by the actual ball hypothesis. It identifies its boundary with the usual oriented sphere. The finitely many disk-face corners can be rounded in their product neighborhoods by replacing each quadrant corner with one fixed monotone smooth arc; transporting the face boundaries and their collars through this rounding leaves a surface diffeomorphic to the original cut surface. Its faces are disjoint smooth disk regions on the sphere. The identifications $g_i$ reverse the boundary orientations induced by $P$: its two sides rejoin to the oriented original surface, so their outward boundary normals point oppositely in the signed surface collar. This is an actual description of the compression-disk cut, not a homological recognition of a ball. [F4, given, construct]

We choose source collars that also remember the transverse curves. An oriented embedded circle in an oriented surface has a smooth transverse vector field near it: in finitely many oriented circle charts choose vectors on one prescribed positive side and combine them with the finite smooth bump localization in [F2]. Along the circle their positive normal components remain positive, so the combination is transverse. The short flow gives $c(p,t)$ for $p$ on that circle and signed small $t$. Its derivative at $t=0$ consists of the tangent and this transverse vector and is invertible. [F2] and compactness give one common width and injectivity after shrinking: a collision sequence at widths tending to zero would limit to one circle point and violate its local inverse. Distinct circles have disjoint such collars. The $\beta$ crossings are finite by transversality and compactness. In a preliminary collar with angular coordinate $s$, each local $\beta$ arc is $s=s_j(t)$ by [F2]. Choose disjoint small angular intervals about its crossings $s_j(0)$ and smooth cutoffs $\chi_j$ supported there and equal to one near those points. The change $$ (s,t)\longmapsto\left(s+\sum_j\chi_j(s)(s_j(t)-s_j(0)),t\right)$$ is a smooth collar diffeomorphism for small signed $t$, because its angular derivative tends uniformly to one. It is understood in the separate local angular lifts, so is periodic globally. Composing the preliminary collar with it makes the actual $j$th $\beta$ arc have constant circle parameter $s_j(0)$ for both signs of $t$. Cut these signed collars at $t=0$ to prescribe paired inward collars on $P$, one with parameter $t\ge0$ and its partner with parameter $-t\le0$, with the same underlying point $p\in\alpha_i$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Construct a standard target cut model $P'$ inside the Riemann sphere. Choose $h$ small pairwise disjoint round closed disks $F_i^+$ strictly in the upper half-plane and their conjugate disks $F_i^-$ strictly in the lower half-plane, all disjoint from the real projective circle. Remove their interiors. Pair their rims by complex conjugation $R(z)=\overline z$. Choose any orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism $b_i^+:\partial E_i^+\to\partial F_i^+$, and set $$b_i^-=R\circ b_i^+\circ g_i^{-1}.$$ This map too preserves the boundary orientation of the cut surfaces, since $R$ and $g_i$ both reverse it. In a disk pair with centers $a_i,\overline{a_i}$ and radius $r_i$, parameterize its target inward collars by $$c_i^+(x,t)=a_i+r_i e^t e^{-ix},\qquad c_i^-(x,t)=\overline{a_i}+r_i e^t e^{ix},\qquad t\ge0.$$ These lie outside the deleted disks and are paired by $R$. Here $x$ is the angular parameter determined by $b_i^+$, so the prescribed map on the negative rim uses exactly the same $x$. Choose all collar widths small enough to be disjoint. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Apply [F1] to realize these boundary assignments and collars by a diffeomorphism $B:P\to P'$. To reduce the spherical regions to its stated planar form, put the stereographic pole inside one chosen source face, and inside its assigned target face for the target parametrization. That face is then the unbounded disk side of its boundary circle; its complement is a bounded smooth Jordan disk, and all remaining faces are finite disjoint disk holes inside it. Thus the outer boundary and all inner boundary assignments are exactly those of [F1]. The prescribed collars transport through these smooth sphere coordinates. The resulting $B$ satisfies $B g_i=R B$ on the paired rims and satisfies the exact paired collar formulas in steps2.1–3.1. Form the quotient $M$ of $P'$ by these finitely many rim identifications. Away from the seams keep its sphere complex charts. Near a positive rim use the local branch $$w_+(z)=i\log((z-a_i)/r_i),$$ and near its paired negative rim use $$w_-(z)=-i\log((z-\overline{a_i})/r_i).$$ On their collars these are $x+it$ and $x-it$ respectively, and they agree on the identified rim. They therefore give one complex coordinate across the seam. Local branch changes add real multiples of $2\pi$, so all seam transitions are holomorphic; their transitions to the interior charts are the displayed holomorphic logarithms. Distinct seam neighborhoods can be disjoint. These charts also give the smooth finite boundary gluing a Hausdorff manifold structure: two points away from an identified pair separate in the compact cut surface; near a seam the signed collar gives the separating local disk. Compactness follows from the quotient of compact $P'$. Hence they define an actual closed Riemann surface, without deriving integrability from an arbitrary smooth almost complex tensor. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The map $B$ descends to a smooth diffeomorphism $\overline B:\Sigma\to M$. In fact its boundary compatibility gives the bijective quotient map, and its prescribed collar formulas identify a source signed collar $(p,t)$ with the target seam chart $$w=x(b_i^+(p))+it.$$ This is a smooth local diffeomorphism across the original $\alpha_i$, with smooth inverse, and off those circles it is already $B$. Transport the complex charts of $M$ by $\overline B$ to get the claimed orientation-compatible Riemann surface structure on the actual $\Sigma$. Conjugation of $P'$ descends to an antiholomorphic involution of $M$: in a seam chart it sends $x+it$ to $x-it$, and away from seams it is ordinary conjugation in sphere charts. Its fixed set is exactly all $h$ seam circles and the real projective circle remaining inside $P'$. No other interior point of $P'$ is identified with its conjugate. Pull this involution back by $\overline B$. Its seam circles are the original $\alpha_i$; the pullback of the extra real projective circle is the embedded disjoint circle $\delta$. This proves the asserted exact fixed set. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

In the source collars from step2.1, a $\beta$ arc through a crossing has constant $p$ and varying signed $t$. The holomorphic seam chart in step5.1 consequently takes that arc to a vertical straight line and $\alpha_i$ to a horizontal straight line. Translating their intersection to zero gives exactly the imaginary and real lines. Shrink the finitely many crossing charts to have disjoint closures and to meet no other attaching curves locally; transversality and the disjointness of curves within each attaching system permit this. For a product-torus generator, its $h$ entries lie on different disjoint $\alpha$ circles and are therefore distinct. Use its disjoint crossing charts as the standard ordered-root chart of the symmetric product. The quotient is injective on this product of disjoint disks, and the elementary-symmetric description is a holomorphic local coordinate there; equivalently every root is simple and its inverse coordinate is holomorphic by the one-variable implicit-function argument. In these actual product coordinates the two product tori are precisely $\mathbb R^h$ and $i\mathbb R^h$. [F2, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

The $h+1$ fixed ovals just constructed satisfy [F3], with one point on each original $\alpha_i$ and the remaining oval $\delta$. It follows that the standard symmetric product has no nonconstant sphere through $T_\alpha$ and no nonconstant smooth disk with boundary there. The torus is an embedded compact totally real product, as verified in [F3]. The last assertion of [F3] then gives its genuine bounded-energy empty neighborhood under full equality of the structure on $T_\alpha$. Every construction above involved a finite number of faces, collars, charts, circle choices and extensions, besides the stated Countable Choice suppliers. This is a model for one attaching system only: no involution fixing transverse $\alpha$ and $\beta$ circles simultaneously, no empty $T_\beta$ disk count for this same surface structure, and no extra ovals for the larger multipointed symmetric product have been inferred. [F3, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct] ∎

First justify neat cut geometry without assuming transversality of the given proper disks. A smooth handlebody means a manifold diffeomorphic to the standard ball with finitely many smooth one-handles. This model embeds in $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$: take a round ball with finitely many disjoint pairs of small boundary windows and join each pair by a disjoint thin tube outside the ball, choosing the core arcs successively in separate heights and shrinking the tubes. Product window coordinates and corner rounding give the standard smooth one-handle attachments. Transport the actual handlebody and the given disks by one such parametrization and embedding. Apply [F4] to these embedded disk witnesses; their supplied ball cuts are in particular topological balls. Pull the new neat witnesses and the resulting cut-ball parametrizations and product collars back to the actual handlebody. Their boundary circles are EXACTLY the original ones, so the surface, the transverse curve system, and every desired complex-model conclusion are unchanged. This changes only auxiliary compression witnesses; it does not claim an ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism converting the original tangency to a transverse intersection. For the neat replacement system parametrize each actual cut ball by the standard ball and its boundary by an oriented sphere. Round its finitely many disk-face corners in their product neighborhoods by a fixed smooth rounded-quadrant profile and transport the face boundaries and their collars through that rounding. The original surface cut along $\gamma$ is thereby a disjoint union of regions $P_a$ in these spheres, each the complement of the interiors of finitely many disjoint smooth disk faces. Pairing faces recovers the original surface. Every $P_a$ has at least one face: the adjacency graph whose vertices are cut balls and whose edges are the original disks is connected because $U$ is connected; if $k>1$ each vertex meets an edge, and if $k=1$ its $m>0$ disks supply faces. Paired rims have orientation-reversing identification maps $g_i$, since they join the two sides of an oriented surface circle. The standard-ball parametrizations used here are supplied by [F4], not inferred merely from a component being a topological ball. [F4, given, construct]

Choose disjoint signed source collars around the $\gamma_i$ which straighten the $\beta$ crossings. To construct one, take finitely many oriented circle charts, combine local vectors pointing to the same positive normal side by the finite bump localization in [F2], and flow the resulting smooth transverse field. The tangent and transverse derivatives at time zero are independent. [F2], compactness and the local inverse give a common collar width and injectivity: any collision sequence at widths tending to zero has a common limiting circle point and contradicts that inverse. In its angular coordinate $s$ and signed normal coordinate $t$, the finitely many transverse $\beta$ arcs are graphs $s=s_j(t)$. With cutoffs $\chi_j$ in disjoint small angular intervals about their distinct crossings, change the collar by $$ (s,t)\longmapsto\left(s+\sum_j\chi_j(s)(s_j(t)-s_j(0)),t\right).$$ Its angular derivative tends uniformly to one as $t\to0$, so it is a collar diffeomorphism after shrinking. It makes those actual arcs have constant $s=s_j(0)$ on both sides of the circle. Each paired face of the cut surface now has the induced inward collar, with the same underlying circle point and opposite signed normal parameters. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

For each $P_a$ take a separate standard Riemann sphere and choose one small round closed disk for each of its faces, with all disks disjoint. Their complement is $P'_a$. For each original disk pair choose a plus and a minus face, possibly in the same sphere, with target disk centers $a_i^+,a_i^-$ and radii $r_i^+,r_i^-$. Pair their rims by the map $H_i$ defined by $$a_i^++r_i^+e^{-ix}\longmapsto a_i^-+r_i^-e^{ix}.$$ It reverses the boundary orientations of the cut surfaces. Choose an orientation-preserving map $b_i^+$ from the source plus rim to its target rim, and define $b_i^-=H_i b_i^+ g_i^{-1}$ on the minus rim; this too preserves boundary orientation. Prescribe the target inward collars $$c_i^+(x,t)=a_i^++r_i^+e^t e^{-ix},\qquad c_i^-(x,t)=a_i^-+r_i^-e^t e^{ix},\qquad t\ge0.$$ Apply [F1] on each component to realize all its assigned maps and collar germs. Indeed a stereographic pole in any one face turns its complement into the bounded outer smooth Jordan region, with the remaining faces its disk holes; do the same in the corresponding target face. Thus this is exactly the planar hypothesis of [F1]. It gives diffeomorphisms $B_a:P_a\to P'_a$, with every paired-rim and collar assignment compatible. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Glue the target rims by the $H_i$. On the complement of the seams keep the standard sphere complex charts. Across the $i$th seam use the local logarithmic branches $$w_+(z)=i\log((z-a_i^+)/r_i^+),\qquad w_-(z)=-i\log((z-a_i^-)/r_i^-).$$ They take the two inward collars to $x+it$ and $x-it$ and agree on the identified rim. They therefore form one chart across it. Changes of a logarithm branch are real translations by multiples of $2\pi$, so the seam transitions are holomorphic; transitions to an interior sphere chart are the displayed holomorphic functions. Distinct seam neighborhoods can be disjoint. The resulting quotient is a compact Hausdorff smooth surface: signed collar disks give its neighborhoods at seams, and compact separation in the finite cut surfaces separates any other pair of nonidentified points. The maps $B_a$ glue to a smooth diffeomorphism from the original $\Sigma$: their collar formulas identify a source signed collar $(p,t)$ with $$w=x(b_i^+(p))+it,$$ so smoothness and smooth inverse hold across every seam as well as off them. Pull back these actual holomorphic charts to define $j$. Its orientation agrees with that of $\Sigma$, since all $B_a$ preserve orientations and the two signed half-collars have the given orientation. On the cut surface its charts restrict exactly to those of $P'_a$, proving the asserted smooth-up-to-boundary conformal identification. In particular integrability is established by written-out holomorphic transitions, not by an unproved isothermal-coordinate theorem. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

At a crossing the source collar in step2.1 has constant $p$ on the $\beta$ arc, so the holomorphic chart in step4.1 is horizontal on $\gamma$ and vertical on $\beta$. Translate their crossing to zero. Shrinking around the finitely many crossings gives disjoint closed charts meeting no other arcs of the same disjoint systems. A product-torus generator has distinct entries on its different $\gamma_i$. Its product of these disjoint crossing disks is an ordered-root coordinate neighborhood for the symmetric product; simple-root holomorphic inversion in [F2] verifies the local inverse. Thus the actual standard symmetric-product structure, with no target modification, has the two tori as $\mathbb R^m$ and $i\mathbb R^m$ in that chart. This proves the full balanced auxiliary model for $m=h+k-1$. No reflection involution on the whole glued surface is asserted: the independently paired boundary reflections need not form one global map. The conclusion supplies no disk index, count or emptiness statement. All face, chart, collar and extension choices are finite in addition to the stated Countable Choice suppliers. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct] ∎
